translations: The first time Kuafu announced he wanted to chase the sun, his tribe was hurrying to pull the grain off the stones before night fell.

The sun was already slipping westward, and mountain shadows stretched into the valley mouth. Children clutched their grain baskets and ran home, while elders urged them to hurry, because as soon as dusk fell, distant beasts and the rugged mountain paths would slip into darkness. Kuafu stood on a high ridge, watching the sun light the fields each day and then rush away again.
“Why does it always go west?” he asked.
An old man answered, “The sun walks its own road, and people live their own days. If you think night comes too fast, harvest your grain earlier.”
“What if I could catch it?”
The elder paused his work. “Then first ask your own shadow if it’s willing. It’s been following you from dawn to dusk and is already tired enough.”

Kuafu looked down, and his long shadow was already stretching over a few grain baskets. The kids quickly moved the baskets aside, fearing the shadow might crush the grain and leave a giant’s outline instead.

The joke didn’t deter Kuafu. He kept watching the sun, memorizing its rise in the east and set in the west; then he climbed the surrounding hills to see where the western road led. The sun gives the world light and heat, and it also firmly separates day from night. Kuafu didn’t want to spend his whole life guessing where the sun went after sunset—he wanted to walk right to the place where it set and see if a person could ever catch that beam of light.

The tribe tried to counsel him: a giant may have big steps, but the world is bigger. Someone suggested waiting on a high mountain for the sun to return—at least he’d save his shoes. Another said he could shout, “Slow down!” to the sun; if it didn’t hear him, there’d still be time to chase later.

Kuafu didn’t argue. He whittled a sturdy wooden staff, tested it on rocks and mud to make sure it could bear climbing and long travel. He packed just enough food for the first stretch and stored water in a skin bag. He didn’t count miles, didn’t use any magical device to measure the sun’s speed, and didn’t recruit anyone to share the chase.
“If you catch it, will you bring the sun back?” a child asked.
“If one person could bring the sun home, everything else would fall into darkness,” Kuafu replied. “I want to catch up to it, not lock it at my doorstep.”
“Then what will you say to it?”
“First catch it, then think about the words.”
The child thought that was an honest plan, except the first part was a bit… huge.

The night before he set out, Kuafu walked the paths around the village once more. Hearth fires went out one by one, and darkness closed in over the valleys. He heard people inside planning tomorrow’s work, and he heard the wind whistling through trees where there was no light. Chasing the sun wasn’t a momentary temper tantrum with the sky; it was his stubborn quest to probe the very edge of light.

He also strapped the water skin to his shoulder and his waist for a test run. The shoulder bag bounced with each stride, the waist one stayed steadier, so he tightened the waist strap again. When the tribe saw him fuss over even a single water skin, they finally understood that “chasing the sun” wasn’t a post‑meal boast—it was a real, foot‑long journey.

At first light, the sun’s ray crept over the eastern peaks, and Kuofu gripped his staff tightly. He didn’t wait for the sun to climb overhead, nor did he hold a long farewell. With each footfall the ground gave a light tremor, and his massive silhouette crossed the edge of the village lands.

The sun moved slowly westward ahead of him, and Kuofu took long strides across the earth. The tribe watched him shrink into the distance until only dust rose on the open plain. Kuofu’s first step toward chasing the sun had landed, and from that moment every question would have to be answered by the road, the heat, and his own strength.
As Kuofu ran across the tribe’s plain, the sun had just slipped past the eastern mountain peaks.

He leapt over field ridges, and the river ditches below looked like shallow lines under his feet. At first some villagers followed, hoping to see him off to the old hunting grounds; halfway there they were left only with waving hands. Aman clutched a green bamboo slip and kept at it the longest, running while scribbling, “Kuofu heads west, strides huge, dust… the recorder can still—”
Kuofu’s next step crossed a ditch, and his silhouette was already far ahead.
The young man lowered his head and finished the sentence: “…still see it.”

He caught up to the ditch’s edge, then leapt over a stretch of forest. The bamboo slips slapped each other in his arms, as eager as their owner. He intended to note every step Kuofu took, only to discover he’d etched three long lines that looked both like a road and like the distance Kuofu had left behind him.
“Wait!” he shouted.

Far behind, Kuofu turned, thinking danger lurked. The youngster, panting, leaned on his leg and said, “No danger—I just wanted to check whether you have to chase the sun all in one day. The sun will be back tomorrow.”
“It comes tomorrow, and it goes today,” Kuofu answered, then kept heading west.

He watched the gap widen again and had to admit he didn’t even know if the sun ever gets tired; Kuofu clearly wasn’t planning to think about the recorder’s comfort. Light‑hearted talk stayed in the early stretch; the road under his feet grew serious fast.

Scrub and loose stones forced Kuofu to adjust his stride. If he took winding paths, the sun kept slipping west; if he rushed straight ahead, he’d break branches and scatter beasts. Kuofu used his staff to brush aside dead wood, leapt over crossable gullies, and skirted any nests or human dwellings. He was chasing the sun, not carving a giant‑only highway through the land.

One gorge was too wide to jump in a single bound. Kuofu laid his staff across the banks, swung his body onto the opposite side, then pulled the staff back in one smooth motion. When the followers later reached the gorge, they could only see the deep gouge left by the staff tip, confirming he hadn’t changed direction. That single crossing added distance and left a trace for others to verify.

Extra rope and thick hide on his shoulders began to slow him down. He left a bundle of warm hide at a stone shelter for later travelers, keeping only the water skin, food, and staff. Lightening his load, his pace quickened again.

The young man raced to the stone shelter following the giant footprints, expecting Kuofu to be resting there. Inside he found only a thick hide. He turned to the green bamboo slip and said, “Good news—caught his clothing. Bad news—clothing won’t let me visit.”

He recorded the direction and footprints on the slip and kept on. From then on Kuofu’s footprints grew farther apart; each landing left a clear dent. On a hard patch he lost his trace, so he climbed a rise to look for kicked‑up dust. By the time he figured it out, Kuofu had already passed the edge of the plain.

The sun was still ahead, its light shifting from pale morning to full blaze. Kuofu didn’t pause to re‑swear an oath now that he’d left the village, nor did he stop to wait for companions. He ran into the empty wilderness; the first leg was over, but the chase had only covered the easiest part.

Aman finally lost Kuofu completely for the first time. He carved “Kuofu entered the western wilds” onto a green bamboo slip, his finger trembling over the knife marks as if afraid the characters might slip away. When he finished, he sat down to catch his breath, leaning against a jutting rock, sweat beads rolling down his forehead like tiny pearl rain. In the distance, Kuofu’s silhouette was already swallowed by a scorching halo, the dust he kicked up swirling into golden whirlpools in the wind.

Aman looked up and saw Kuofu’s long robe glittering under the blazing sun, like a giant burning snake. The snake would lift its head now and then, its mouth seeming to shout, “Sun, hurry up, let me catch you!” Aman couldn’t help but laugh, muttering, “If he drags the sun home, we’ll be sun‑baked every day!” Before he finished, Kuofu had already left deep footprints on a sand dune, some of the stones in the prints turned red‑hot, like roasted chestnuts.

Aman stood up, but the scorching ground made his steps wobble; he braced against the rock, trying not to turn into a charred stick himself. He kept following Kuofu’s footprints, the sand sizzling softly with each step as if mocking his sluggish pace. “My speed would make a snail laugh,” he whispered. In his haste he knocked the bamboo slip against a stone, a thin crack spider‑webbing across the edge, as if the sun’s heat had baked a tiny bite into it. He quickly brushed the ink off the crack, muttering, “Even this slip wants to chase the sun with me—talk about bad luck.”

He kept tracking, his steps growing heavier, the hot air like a tangible rope tightening around his chest. Kuofu had vanished ahead, leaving only rolling heat waves that rose like massive tides. Aman looked up at the sky, saw the sun hanging high, its glare cutting like a knife, and grumbled, “This sun is ruthless—won’t even leave me a shadow.” He clutched the bamboo slip to his chest, afraid the wind might snatch it away.
